notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 25 below. There are some gaps you should know about first:

- **Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Pentecostal-specific sites (pneumareview, ag.org, samstorms) and bibleodyssey essays:** I found nothing that discusses this chapter, apart from a short Bible Odyssey dictionary entry on Phinehas.
- **Prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this chapter, so that section is left out.
- **Tradition labels:** Where I name a commentator's tradition (for example Wesley as Methodist or Calvin as Reformed), that comes from general knowledge, not from the pages themselves.
- **No citation tags:** Points drawn from the full OCA page and the Bible Hub verse 6 page have a URL but no citation tag.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Gill says Shittim (Abel-shittim) was Israel's last stop in the wilderness. Falling into sin right on the border of Canaan made it worse. He adds that the daughters of Midian were also involved (see v. 6), and that it happened through Balaam's advice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/25.htm
- Wesley makes the same point about the timing. Of Moab and Midian he says "both these people being confederated in this wicked design, the one is put for the other". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- Guzik sees ingratitude here. God had just protected Israel from Balaam and Balak's attempts to curse them, and Israel's harlotry, both sexual and spiritual, was their ungrateful response. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/

**v. 2:** Wesley explains the "sacrifices" as feasts made from parts of the offerings. Eating them "was reckoned a participation in the worship of that God". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- Matthew Henry says that by first committing sexual sin the men "debauched their consciences" and were then easily drawn to bow to idols. He also thinks the sexual sin was probably part of Baal-peor worship itself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_025.cfm
- Henry links this to Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 10:20 against eating food offered to idols. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_025.cfm

**v. 3:** Precept Austin explains that the word "joined" (yoked) pictures two animals yoked together, and shows how flagrantly obstinate the rebellion was. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- Wesley offers two explanations of the name Peor: the hill Peor, or a verb meaning "to open, uncover", referring to the idol's obscene posture or the filthy rites of its worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- JFB says "The real name of the idol was Chemosh," which made this a double offence: idolatry and licentiousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-25.html
- Walter Kaiser (quoted on Precept Austin) suspects the cult "also involved veneration for the dead". https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- Guzik notes that Balaam had prophesied from the high places of Baal, possibly from this same place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/

**v. 4:** Older commentators disagree over who was to be executed:
- **Gill** follows Jewish interpreters: the heads of the people were to *judge* and hang the guilty, not be hanged themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/25.htm
- **Poole and Wesley** think the guilty leaders themselves were executed. Leaders were singled out because their sin was "more odious and mischievous in them". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- **JFB** says those executed were the subordinate officers, and that criminals were first killed and *then* hung up. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-25.html
- **Ellicott** suggests the chiefs had allowed this behaviour, judging from Zimri's case. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-4.htm
- On "against the sun": Wesley says it means publicly, because the sin was public, and quickly, before sundown. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm

**v. 5:** Poole says "his men" means those under each judge's charge. The seventy elders shared the work of governing among them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-5.htm
- Guzik says Moses wouldn't accept that decay in the culture. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/numbers/numbers-25.cfm

**v. 6:** From the Bible Hub verse 6 page (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-6.htm):
- Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary note the Hebrew says "*the* Midianite woman". Barnes thinks her high rank shows Zimri had been deliberately targeted.
- Barnes says the plague had already started and the more God-fearing people were interceding at the tabernacle.
- Gill notes that "behold" marks the act's astonishing boldness.
- The Geneva Bible reads the weeping as repentance.
- Keil & Delitzsch explain that the word for "tent" refers to the inner sleeping room of a larger tent.

Guzik quotes Allen: the definite article marks her out as a pivotal player, perhaps the high priestess of the religion at Baal Peor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/

**vv. 7–8:** Guzik insists that Phinehas was not a vigilante and his act does not justify vigilantism; Numbers 3–4 made priests responsible for guarding the tabernacle against intruders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/
- Gill points to 1 Chronicles 9:20: Phinehas had civil as well as priestly authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/25.htm
- Gill also says the plague stopping right after the act shows that God approved of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/25.htm
- Constable says the act should be seen as divine judgment on this attitude and action, not as murder. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/25-7.html
- Constable also says that in this story Moses is remarkably ineffective in the face of a blatant transgression. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/25-7.html
- Matthew Henry says the people's weeping and praying did not succeed until this "necessary justice" was done. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_025.cfm

**v. 9 (24,000 versus Paul's 23,000 in 1 Corinthians 10:8):** Three explanations:
- **Gill:** Moses counts everyone who died, including those hanged. Paul counts only those who "fell", and the hanged may have numbered about 1,000. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/25.htm
- **Wesley:** simply notes the difference. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- **A source on Precept Austin:** takes 1 Corinthians 10:8 to be about the golden calf, not Peor. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- Guzik adds that the death toll must have delighted Balak; Balaam had succeeded in getting Israel to curse themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Num/Num-25.cfm

**vv. 10–11:** Keil & Delitzsch say the phrase means not "zeal for me," but "my zeal," the zeal of Jehovah with which Phinehas was filled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-13.htm
- Ellicott says Phinehas's full family line is repeated to show he was not a private individual, but one invested with public authority. https://biblehub.com/numbers/25-11.htm
- The NET note (quoted on Precept Austin) defines zeal as a passionate intensity to protect or preserve divine or social institutions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- Gill sees Phinehas as a type (foreshadowing) of Christ, whose zeal for God's house "ate him up" (Psalm 69:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/25.htm

**v. 12:** Wesley explains why it is called a "covenant of peace":
- Phinehas had made peace between God and the people.
- The priest's main job is to mediate between God and people and keep that peace.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm

**v. 13:** The Pulpit Commentary says God's vengeance through Phinehas was accepted by God as a propitiation (lit., a covering) for the sin of the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-25.html
- The NET note says that because the sinners themselves died, he dispensed with any animal sacrifice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- Ellicott traces the history: Phinehas succeeded Eleazar, and after an interruption in Eli's time the office was restored by Solomon to Zadok, Phinehas's descendant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-13.htm

**vv. 14–15:** JFB says Zimri's high rank is mentioned to show how fearless Phinehas was, since there might be numerous avengers of his blood. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-25.html
- Guzik gives the meanings of the names: Zimri ('my remembrance') and Cozbi ('my lie' or 'deception'). Both were children of leaders who should have known better. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/
- The Pulpit Commentary says their names, families and rank are recorded so that an immortality of infamy is theirs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-25.html

**vv. 16–18:** Wesley asks why Midian and not Moab. He thinks Midian was probably more guilty, because they had persuaded Balak to send for Balaam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- On the "wiles", Wesley says Midian offered kinship and friendship instead of war, as a way to bring on Israel the curse Balaam could not deliver directly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- The NET note says "harass" is repeated so the punishment is talionic (it matches the offence). https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- The command is carried out in Numbers 31, where Balaam is also killed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-25-commentary
- The Expositor's Bible argues the point is the sacredness of morality, not of Israel, and that Jehovah is not revengeful, but just. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/numbers/25.htm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 7–8 (can anyone follow Phinehas's example?)** Every Protestant voice I found agrees he must not be copied by private individuals. They differ on *why* his act was legitimate:
- **Reformed (Calvin):** anyone who copies Phinehas "in his preposterous zeal" boasts in vain unless he shall be thoroughly assured of the command of God. In other words, a direct divine command is what counts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/25-7.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Phinehas was probably one of the judges Moses had ordered to act, so the story gives no countenance at all to private persons. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_025.cfm
- **Methodist (Wesley):** combines several grounds. Phinehas had great authority, acted after Moses' command and with his consent, and also by the special direction of God's spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- **Charles Simeon:** applies the passage to rulers. Magistrates hold the sword and should use it against wrongdoers. He then points to Christ, who gave *his own* life rather than taking others'. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/shh/numbers-25.html
- **Coffman:** argues that later Jewish law wrongly built on this episode. God certainly was not commending him for taking justice into his own hands; it was his zeal that God commended. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/25-7.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** grounds it in the priests' duty to guard the tabernacle (see vv. 7–8 above). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/

**v. 13 ("permanent" priesthood: conditional or irrevocable?)**
- **Wesley:** the promise was conditional, and therefore might be made void, as happened when the priesthood passed to Eli's line for a time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/25.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** it was given in an irrevocable form, since God never breaks a covenant that He has made. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-13.htm

**v. 13 (Phinehas and faith)** A Precept Austin word study calls Phinehas an OT example of "justification by faith", with his deed as the outworking of faith. This draws on Psalm 106:31, "reckoned to him for righteousness". https://www.preceptaustin.org/shalom_-_definition

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **Peake's Commentary:** fragments of two distinct narratives have been united. Verses 1–5 come from the "JE" source, verses 6–18 from the Priestly source ("P"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-25.html
- Peake also says the Phinehas story is designed to support the exclusive claim to the priesthood of the descendants of Zadok. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-25.html
- **Cambridge Bible:** dates verses 6–15 to after the exile and thinks the beginning of the plague story has been lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/25-6.htm
- **Bible Odyssey:** says the act stayed the wrath of God against the people and earned a covenant of eternal priesthood. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/phinehas/

**Catholic**
- **Haydock:** God did not promise that no interruption should take place; He granted a perpetual right which they might forfeit by misconduct. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/25-13.html
- Haydock also warns that the Zealots abused this kind of liberty during the last siege of Jerusalem. He argues Phinehas was either a judge or inspired by God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/25-13.html
- **The Knox translation on New Advent:** renders "into the tent" as "into the place of shame". The Vulgate reads *in lupanar* (a brothel). https://www.newadvent.org/bible/num025.htm

**Orthodox**
- The OCA honours "Righteous Phineas" as a saint on March 12. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/1949/03/12/100788-righteous-phineas-the-grandson-of-aaron
- Its account says many Israelites repented when they saw God's wrath. It adds that Phinehas later led the army against Midian, was unanimously chosen high priest after Eleazar, and that the high priesthood continued in his line. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/1949/03/12/100788-righteous-phineas-the-grandson-of-aaron

**Modern popular teaching (one example)**
- Carson's Gospel Coalition devotional admits the act will "evoke horror". He argues that under a covenant where adultery and idolatry carried the death penalty, his action appears more principled than barbaric, because it saved countless lives. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/numbers-25-psalm-68-isaiah-15-1-peter-3/
